results.finding: Screening with CTA or MRA is recommended for people with two or more family members with intracranial aneurysm or SAH. Hypertension should be treated and smoking stopped in patients with an unruptured aneurysm; size, location, growth, age and family history inform the choice between treatment and surveillance.
results.source: Thompson BG, Brown RD Jr, Amin-Hanjani S, et al. Guidelines for the management of patients with unruptured intracranial aneurysms (AHA/ASA). Stroke 2015;46:2368-2400

results.finding: Population, hypertension, age, size, earlier SAH from another aneurysm and site predict 5-year rupture risk; middle cerebral artery site and hypertension each add points.
results.source: Greving JP, Wermer MJH, Brown RD Jr, et al. Development of the PHASES score for prediction of risk of rupture of intracranial aneurysms: a pooled analysis of six prospective cohort studies. Lancet Neurol 2014;13:59-66

output.summary: Screening is recommended when two or more relatives have an aneurysm or SAH; management of an unruptured aneurysm weighs rupture predictors, and hypertension and smoking are the modifiable ones.

Do not add verapamil to propranolol
required_recommendations: Confirm sporadic hemiplegic migraine (motor and speech aura with headache, normal MRI) and explain the aneurysm as a separate finding that does not cause the attacks

Refer to the neurovascular multidisciplinary team for the 4 mm left MCA bifurcation aneurysm to choose between surveillance imaging and treatment, taking into account two affected first-degree relatives, hypertension and the MCA site (PHASES 3) (AHA/ASA 2015)
Confirm his blood pressure with home or ambulatory readings and treat it to below 130/80 mmHg: hypertension is a modifiable rupture risk factor
Advise him to remain a non-smoker, keep alcohol within 14 units a week and avoid stimulants such as cocaine and amphetamines
Explain the warning symptoms of aneurysm rupture (sudden thunderclap headache, collapse, neck stiffness) and the need to call emergency services

Optimise prevention: propranolol 40 mg twice daily is a modest dose but his pulse is 62; either increase it if pulse and BP allow, or switch to a hemiplegic-migraine preventive such as verapamil, lamotrigine or acetazolamide, never adding verapamil to propranolol
Treat attacks with an NSAID (for example naproxen 500 mg) or paracetamol with an antiemetic

avoided_actions.rationale: A repeat head CT adds nothing: he had a normal CT, and MRI with MRA answers both the structural and the aneurysm question without radiation.
Lumbar puncture is not indicated: there has been no thunderclap or sentinel headache suggesting SAH, and no suspicion of infection.
Echocardiography is not indicated: there is no infarct or embolic event, and PFO screening is not part of the migraine work-up.
Repeat cardiac monitoring is not indicated: a 24-hour Holter was normal and the attacks are migraine aura, not embolic events.

findings.result: Five stereotyped attacks in 18 months; two of them on propranolol 40 mg twice daily.
Right hand and arm weakness with clumsiness, followed after several minutes by word-finding difficulty; the deficit builds up over 20-25 minutes. No visual or sensory symptoms reported.
20-35 minutes per attack, with full recovery of strength and speech.
Each attack is followed within minutes by a severe (9/10) left-sided throbbing headache with nausea and photophobia lasting 10-16 hours.
Fully reversible motor weakness with fully reversible speech disturbance (ICHD-3 1.2.3 B met). No first- or second-degree relative with hemiplegic migraine (sporadic form, 1.2.3.2).
Father: aneurysmal SAH (left MCA) 8 weeks ago. Sister: unruptured 3 mm posterior communicating artery aneurysm and migraine without aura.
Mild hypertension, not treated (BP 136/84 mmHg on propranolol); non-smoker; 6-8 units of alcohol a week.
Normal language, cranial nerves, power, reflexes, sensation, coordination and gait. Pulse 62 on propranolol.

Motor aura: present. Two first-degree relatives with intracranial aneurysm or aneurysmal SAH: present. Thunderclap onset, systemic symptoms, onset after 50, deficit outside the attacks, positional or Valsalva trigger and papilloedema: absent.

clinical_assessment.impression: Recurrent stereotyped motor and speech aura followed by migrainous headache, meeting ICHD-3 1.2.3.2 sporadic hemiplegic migraine (5 attacks; 5 of 6 criterion C characteristics). Red flags present: motor aura and a family history of intracranial aneurysm in two first-degree relatives.

scores.ICHD-3 criterion C characteristics met: 5 of 6 (gradual spread, succession, duration within the motor limit, unilateral, headache within 60 min)

alternatives: Acute: NSAID (for example naproxen 500 mg) or paracetamol, with an antiemetic
Prevention in hemiplegic migraine: verapamil (instead of, not with, propranolol), lamotrigine, acetazolamide, topiramate, flunarizine where licensed
contraindications: Triptans and ergot derivatives: avoid in hemiplegic migraine (product labels; no safety data in motor aura).
interactions: Propranolol + rizatriptan: propranolol raises rizatriptan levels by about 70%; the label dose is 5 mg. No such interaction with sumatriptan.
Propranolol + verapamil: additive negative chronotropic and dromotropic effects with risk of bradycardia, AV block and hypotension; avoid the combination, and allow a washout when switching.
Propranolol + topiramate: no clinically relevant interaction.
Propranolol + paracetamol or NSAIDs: no clinically relevant interaction; regular NSAIDs can blunt the antihypertensive effect.
sumatriptan.proposed: Acute and preventive migraine treatment in a man on propranolol 40 mg twice daily (pulse 62) with an unruptured intracranial aneurysm
sumatriptan.summary: Triptans and ergots are avoided in hemiplegic migraine; verapamil must not be added to propranolol; rizatriptan, if ever used with propranolol, is limited to 5 mg.
warnings: No data on triptan use with an unruptured intracranial aneurysm; the restriction here comes from the hemiplegic migraine.
Propranolol dose increases are limited by a resting pulse of 62.

additional_observations: Technique: non-contrast 3 T brain MRI with T1, T2, FLAIR, DWI/ADC and susceptibility-weighted imaging.
No restricted diffusion; no acute or chronic infarct.
No haemorrhage, microbleed, superficial siderosis, cavernoma or arteriovenous malformation.
Ventricles, sulci and white matter normal for age. No mass.
mri.impression: Normal brain MRI. No infarct, haemorrhage, vascular malformation or mass.

patient.history_present_illness:
A 36-year-old Black British man presented to the neurology clinic for a second opinion. He has had five episodes over the past 18 months of right-sided arm weakness, clumsiness and difficulty with word finding, lasting 20-35 minutes, each followed by a severe left-sided throbbing headache rated 9/10 with marked nausea and photophobia lasting 10-16 hours. The first episode was assessed at the emergency department and was diagnosed as 'likely TIA or hemiplegic migraine.' A normal CT head and a normal 24-hour Holter were performed. He was subsequently seen by a neurologist who diagnosed hemiplegic migraine and started propranolol 40 mg BID. Two further episodes occurred on propranolol.

New information from this visit: his father (aged 64) had a subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH) 8 weeks ago from a ruptured left MCA aneurysm, and last month his sister was found to have a small unruptured aneurysm on screening MRA. The patient is therefore seeking screening for intracranial aneurysm.

On re-review of his episodes: the motor and language deficit develops gradually over approximately 20-25 minutes, which he confirms on careful questioning. He has no family history of hemiplegic migraine. His sister has typical migraine without aura. He has mild hypertension (BP today 136/84). He is a non-smoker, drinks 6-8 units of alcohol a week. He has no prior imaging of the intracranial vessels; only a CT head was performed acutely.
